opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few areas I'd highlight. The first, unsurprisingly given what I work on, is AI control: research on how we could safely use and get useful work out of AI systems even if they're actively trying to subvert our safety measures. I think this is pretty neglected relative to how important it is. Most safety work is oriented around making the model not misaligned in the first place, which is great, but we should also have a plan for the case where we fail at that and can't tell. Control is nice because it's fairly tractable. You can run concrete experiments today with red teams and blue teams, and it doesn't require solving deep conceptual problems.

Within control, I'm particularly excited about things like better monitoring setups, studying how to make protocols robust to collusion between AI instances, and figuring out how to evaluate whether your control measures actually work. That last part, control evaluations, seems really important for labs to be able to make credible safety cases.

Second, I think model organisms of misalignment deserve more work. That means constructing or finding examples of AIs that exhibit things like scheming, alignment faking, or reward hacking in ways that generalize badly, and then studying them. Part of the value is scientific: we learn what conditions produce these behaviors and whether our detection techniques catch them. Part of it is that it gives us better evidence to show people about whether these threat models are real.

Third, I'd point to work on detecting and preventing egregious misalignment more directly, things like probing for deceptive cognition, or "lie detection" style approaches, as well as interpretability that's aimed at answering practical safety questions rather than full mechanistic understanding. I'm somewhat more skeptical of ambitious interpretability paying off in time, but targeted, pragmatic uses seem promising.

And then a somewhat different category: I think there should be more work on how we'd actually use AIs to do safety research, essentially handing off alignment work to AI systems. If things go fast, a lot of the safety research that gets done will be done by AIs, so figuring out how to elicit good work from them, how to check it, and how to avoid getting sabotaged seems really important and underinvested in.

Lastly, there's security-adjacent work, like preventing model weight exfiltration and making sure AIs can't escape or set up rogue deployments inside labs. That's not always thought of as "technical AI safety," but I think it matters a lot.

r002.rationale: It discusses using AI systems to do safety research, but does not recommend training AIs to make wiser decisions than humans.

r003.rationale: It mentions probing for deceptive cognition and lie-detection approaches, but does not clearly specify probing model internals to detect misaligned actions.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few areas that stand out to me as pretty neglected relative to how important they seem.

The first one is what I'd broadly call AI control. The basic idea is: suppose you're deploying a model that's quite capable, and you can't rule out that it's misaligned and actively trying to subvert your safety measures. Can you still get useful work out of it while keeping the risk low? That means things like monitoring untrusted models with trusted but weaker models, auditing suspicious actions, designing protocols where the model can't easily sabotage things without getting caught. I think this is important because it doesn't require you to have solved alignment. It's a backstop. And I think there's a lot of pretty tractable empirical work here that just hasn't been done, especially as we move toward models doing long-horizon agentic tasks in real deployment settings.

Related to that, I'd love to see more work on what you might call "model organisms" of misalignment. So deliberately constructing models that have scheming-like or reward-hacking behaviours, in a controlled way, so that we can actually study whether our detection and mitigation techniques work. Right now a lot of safety research is operating somewhat blind because we don't have good test cases. If you want to know whether your interpretability tool or your monitoring setup catches a model that's pretending to be aligned, you kind of need a model that's pretending to be aligned to test it on.

A third area is the science of understanding when and why models generalise in undesirable ways out of training. We saw some of this with the alignment faking work: models reasoning about the training process and strategically behaving differently depending on whether they think they're being observed. I think we have a pretty poor understanding of how likely these behaviours are to arise naturally, what properties of training make them more or less likely, and how they scale. That seems like a core scientific question that's getting less attention than it deserves relative to, say, interpretability.

And then I'd put in a word for evaluations, but specifically evaluations of capabilities relevant to safety: can the model sabotage research subtly, can it coordinate with other copies of itself, can it tell when it's being evaluated versus deployed. These are the capabilities that determine how much you can trust your other safety measures. I think there's a tendency to treat evals as a kind of compliance exercise, but done well they're actually load-bearing for the whole strategy.

I'd also say, somewhat more meta: I think there's not enough work that takes the perspective of "we might only have a few years, the labs are going to deploy these systems regardless, what's the cheapest set of measures that substantially reduces risk." A lot of research is optimised for being interesting or for producing a nice paper rather than for being the thing you'd actually implement at a lab under time pressure. I'd like to see more people thinking in terms of concrete safety cases and what would actually move the needle on those.

astra-6.text:
I’d probably highlight AI control: trying to ensure that we can get useful work out of powerful AI systems even if those systems aren’t reliably acting in our interests. That seems like an important complement to trying to make the systems aligned in the first place.

For example, suppose you’re using an AI to write code, and you’re worried it might deliberately introduce a subtle security vulnerability. Can you use a weaker, more trusted model to review its work? Which parts need human review? Can you restrict the system’s access so that a mistake in your defenses doesn’t immediately become catastrophic? You can study these questions experimentally, with one team trying to cause failures and another trying to prevent them.

A related area is evaluating whether our safety measures actually work against a system that’s trying to undermine them. It’s relatively easy to show that a monitor catches obvious bad behavior. It’s much harder to establish that it would catch strategically chosen bad behavior from a capable model that knows how the monitor works.

I’d also like to see more work on making AI useful for alignment research itself. There’s potentially a lot of value in automating parts of that research, but then you need ways to check the resulting work without simply trusting the system that produced it.

The common thread is that I’d like more research that makes its assumptions explicit and tests a concrete safety argument. What capability level are you considering? What do you trust? And what would have to go wrong for the proposed approach to fail?

sol-6.1.text:
I think one area that deserves more work is AI control: how do we make sure that powerful AI systems can’t cause catastrophic harm, even if they’re actively trying to? That’s a somewhat different question from how we make them want to do the right thing in the first place.

For example, suppose you’re using an AI to write code, and you’re worried it might insert a subtle backdoor. Can you use a weaker, more trusted model to review its work? When should you escalate to a human? And how do you test whether that whole setup actually works against an AI that’s trying to evade it?

I’d also like to see more work on evaluating whether our safety techniques work when models are deliberately undermining them. A model performing well on an ordinary evaluation doesn’t necessarily tell you how it behaves when it understands the situation and has a reason to hide what it can do.

More broadly, I think there’s a lot of value in taking a concrete threat model and trying to build and test a complete defense against it. That forces you to confront the places where your assumptions might fail, and it can make the research much more directly useful for decisions about deployment.
